title: Matter and its properties
summary: Learn about mass, volume, density, strength, adhesion, and capillary action.
cards.0.p: Anything that has mass and volume is matter. Mass, volume, and inertia are common properties found in all matter. Density, melting point, and conductivity are distinguishing properties that identify a substance.
cards.0.once.soru: Which one is found in all matter?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: All matter has mass and volume. So mass does not identify a substance, and it is a common property.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: A magnet attracts iron but not wood. So not all matter is magnetic.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: Copper conducts electricity, and plastic does not. So conductivity changes from one substance to another.
cards.0.key: Inertia is the tendency of an object to keep its state of motion. You will see the details in Newton's laws.
cards.1.p: Mass is the amount of matter. It is measured with an equal-arm balance and does not change from place to place. Volume is the space that matter takes up. 1 L = 1 dm³ and 1 mL = 1 cm³.
cards.1.key: Mass and weight are not the same thing. On the Moon your mass stays the same, but your weight (the force of gravity on you) is smaller.
cards.2.p: The mass of a unit volume is called density, given by ρ = m / V (g/cm³). A nail and a door made of iron have the same density. So density identifies a substance.
cards.2.key: The density of water is 1 g/cm³, which is 1000 kg/m³.
cards.2.etk.soru: Change the mass and the volume. How does the density change? The density of water is 1 g/cm³.
cards.2.etk.yorum.0.1: This substance is less dense than water. An object made of it floats in water.
cards.2.etk.yorum.1.1: The density of this substance equals that of water. The object stays suspended in water.
cards.2.etk.yorum.2.1: This substance is denser than water. An object made of it sinks in water.
cards.3.p: The mass–volume graph of a substance is a straight line through the origin. The slope of the line is m/V, which is the density. The steeper the line, the denser the substance.
cards.3.key: If the axes are swapped (a V–m graph), the slope is 1/ρ. A density–volume graph is a horizontal line.
cards.4.p: The density of a mixture is ρ = mtotal / Vfinal. The result lies between the two densities and is closer to that of the substance with more volume. For equal volumes the density of the mixture is (ρ₁ + ρ₂) / 2.
cards.4.svg#8: if volume is unchanged: V final = V₁ + V₂
cards.4.key: When water and alcohol mix, the volume shrinks a little. So V₁ + V₂ is only an approximation.
cards.5.p: Matter expands when heated. Its mass stays the same, its volume increases, and its density decreases. Water is an exception, because it is densest at 4 °C.
cards.5.once.soru: A metal ball expands a little when heated. What happens to its density?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: The mass stays the same and the volume increases. So ρ = m / V gets smaller.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: The mass does not increase, the volume does. When the divisor grows, the result shrinks.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: The volume changed. Since the mass stayed the same, the ratio changes too.
cards.6.p: If all the dimensions of an object double, its cross-sectional area becomes 4 times larger and its weight 8 times larger. So its strength is cut in half. That is why an elephant has thick legs.
cards.6.key: If the dimensions grow k times, the strength drops to 1/k.
cards.6.once.soru: You double all the sides of a cube. How many times larger does its volume become?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: Volume is the product of three sides, so it grows 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times. The cross-sectional area grows only 2 × 2 = 4 times.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: Each side doubles, but volume multiplies three sides.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: 4 times is the growth of the cross-sectional area. For volume the third side is multiplied in too.
cards.7.p: The attraction between particles of the same kind is called cohesion, and between particles of different kinds adhesion. Water adheres strongly to glass, so it wets the glass. Mercury does not wet glass.
cards.8.p: Particles at the surface are pulled only from below and from the sides. So the surface behaves like a stretched film. This is called surface tension. Heat and detergent reduce surface tension.
cards.8.svg#0: the water surface acts like a stretched film
cards.8.svg#1: a water strider does not sink
cards.8.once.soru: A water strider walks on water without sinking. What makes this possible?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.yazi: The stretched surface of the water
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: The water particles at the surface hold each other tightly. The surface carries the insect like a thin film.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: The insect walks on still water too, so no current is needed.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: Every living thing has mass. It is the surface of the water that carries the insect.
cards.9.p:
• Mass, volume, and inertia are common properties. Density is a distinguishing property.
• Density is ρ = m / V, and it equals the slope of the mass–volume graph.
• For a mixture ρ = mtotal / Vfinal.
• If the size grows k times, the strength drops to 1/k.
• Cohesion and adhesion explain surface tension and capillary action.
quiz.0.q: Put each property in the right group.
quiz.0.e: Mass, volume, inertia, and being made of particles are found in all matter. Density, melting and boiling points, and conductivity change from one substance to another and identify it.
quiz.1.q: 200 cm³ of a liquid with density 1 g/cm³ is mixed with 100 cm³ of a liquid with density 4 g/cm³. If the volume does not change on mixing, what is the density of the mixture, in g/cm³?
quiz.1.e: The total mass is 200·1 + 100·4 = 600 g, and the final volume is 300 cm³. The density is 600 / 300 = 2 g/cm³. The result is closer to the density of the liquid with more volume.
quiz.2.q: Match each event with the idea that explains it.
quiz.2.ciftler.1.0: A paper towel soaking up water
quiz.2.e: The stretched surface carries the water strider. Water rising in thin channels is called capillary action. Water wets glass because its adhesion to glass is greater than its cohesion. In mercury cohesion is greater, so the surface is convex.
quiz.3.q: If all the sides of a cube are made 3 times longer, how does its strength change?
quiz.3.e: The cross-sectional area becomes 9 times and the volume 27 times larger. Strength depends on the ratio of cross-section to volume, so it drops to 9/27 = 1/3.
quiz.3.y.0: Strength does not grow when the side triples. The cross-sectional area grows 9 times and the volume 27 times, so their ratio shrinks.
quiz.3.y.1: Area and volume grow at different rates. The ratio of cross-sectional area to volume is inversely proportional to the side length.
quiz.3.y.3: You shrank the ratio by the square of the side. The area becomes 9 times and the volume 27 times larger, and 9/27 = 1/3.
A:ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Weigh, pour, mix, and find the density yourself.
A:adimlar.0.metin: One pan of an equal-arm balance holds 1 kg of iron, and the other holds 1 kg of cotton. What happens when you pull out the supports?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: What happens when the pans are released?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: An equal-arm balance compares masses, and both are 1 kg (ignoring the buoyancy of air). The cotton takes up far more space, but a large volume does not mean a large mass.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Iron seems heavy because it fits in a small space, but the masses are equal.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The cotton takes up more space. But a large volume does not mean a large mass.
A:adimlar.1.metin: You pour water into a graduated cylinder, and the scale shows only the mass of the water. Change the volume of the water and make the mass 50 g. Watch the ratio m / V as you do.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: 50 cm³ of water came to 50 g. When the volume changed, the mass changed in the same proportion, but the ratio m / V stayed at 1 g/cm³. So density does not depend on the amount of a substance.
A:adimlar.2.metin: We plotted the mass of three substances against their volume. Each one makes a straight line through the origin.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: Which substance has the highest density?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: A has the steepest line, so it has the most mass for the same volume. A is aluminum (2.7 g/cm³), B is water (1 g/cm³), and C is wood (about 0.5 g/cm³).
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: B's line has a medium slope. At the same volume, say 20 cm³, which one has more mass?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: C's line is the shallowest. It has the least mass for the same volume, so its density is the lowest.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Change the density of the object and leave it suspended in the water.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: When the (average) density of the object equals that of water, the object stays suspended. If it is lower the object floats, and if it is higher the object sinks. For hollow objects the average density is what counts. That is why a steel ship floats, and you will see the details in the Buoyancy topic.
A:adimlar.4.metin: You add alcohol (0.8 g/cm³) to 100 cm³ of water (1 g/cm³). Set the amount of alcohol and make the density of the mixture 0.9 g/cm³.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: When you mix equal volumes, the result is the average of the two densities. (100 + 80) g ÷ 200 cm³ = 0.9 g/cm³.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Water adheres to glass more strongly than it holds on to its own particles. You dip three glass tubes into water.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: In which tube does the water rise highest?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Water climbs by adhering to the glass, and the thinner the tube, the higher it rises. This is called capillary action. It is why water rises in plants and why a paper towel gets wet. Mercury, which does not adhere to glass, drops lower in a thin tube.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: In a wide tube the water to be pulled up is much heavier. Adhesion cannot hold it up.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The height depends on how thin the tube is.
A:kapanis.0: Mass and volume are common properties found in all matter. Density is a distinguishing property that identifies a substance.
A:kapanis.1: Density is ρ = m / V. On a mass–volume graph the slope of the line gives the density, and a steeper line means a denser substance.
A:kapanis.2: An object whose average density is lower than water's floats, one with equal density stays suspended, and one with higher density sinks.
A:kapanis.3: The density of a mixture is ρ = m<sub>total</sub> / V<sub>final</sub>. The result lies between the two densities.
A:kapanis.4: The difference between adhesion and cohesion leads to capillary action. Water rises higher in a thinner tube.
